\section{Layered Architecture in Michelangelo}
\label{sec:layered-architecture}

This section analyses Michelangelo's backbone style, the \textbf{layered
architecture}: its definition (\Cref{sec:layered-style}), how Michelangelo maps
onto it (\Cref{sec:layered-mapping}), how the layers communicate
(\Cref{sec:layered-communication}), which other styles live inside the layers
(\Cref{sec:layered-other-styles}) and how well the style serves the platform
(\Cref{sec:layered-evaluation}).

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The Layered Architecture Style}
\label{sec:layered-style}

A layered architecture splits a system into horizontal layers. Each layer offers
services to the layer above and uses services of the layer
below~\cite{buschmann1996}. The core rule is a one-way \emph{allowed-to-use}
relation: a layer may use the layers beneath it, never those above
it~\cite{bass2021}. Richards and Ford call the style \emph{technically
partitioned}: the system is divided by technical role rather than by business
domain~\cite{richards2020}. A \emph{closed} layer cannot be skipped and so
isolates changes; an \emph{open} layer can be bypassed~\cite{richards2020}.

\textbf{Benefits:} easy to understand and split among teams; a layer can be
replaced behind a stable interface; lower layers are
reusable~\cite{richards2020,bass2021}.
\textbf{Liabilities:} each crossed layer adds latency; cross-cutting changes touch
every layer; strict layering feels rigid~\cite{richards2020,bass2021}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Mapping Michelangelo onto Layers}
\label{sec:layered-mapping}

In 2017, Michelangelo's components ran on ``a mix of open source systems and
components built in-house'' such as HDFS, Spark, Samza and Cassandra, managed by
an API tier, web UI and workflow system~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. In 2018 Uber
began ``factoring out Michelangelo's infrastructure into an explicit
infrastructure layer''~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}. By 2024 the architecture is
described as \textbf{three planes} (control, offline data and online data) built
on a layer of \textbf{plug-and-play components}~\cite{wang2024predictive}. To
these \textbf{we add two layers of our own}, built from components Uber names: an
\emph{experience layer} on top and an \emph{infrastructure layer} at the bottom
(\Cref{fig:layered-view,tab:layers}).

    Each arrow means ``uses'' (top-down only). The offline and online data
    planes are peers inside layer L3.}
  \label{fig:layered-view}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Control plane (L4).} It ``defines user-facing APIs and manages the
lifecycle of all entities in the system'', following the Kubernetes Operator
pattern and API conventions~\cite{wang2024predictive}. Its standard entities are
Project, Pipeline, PipelineRun, Model, Revision, InferenceServer and
Deployment~\cite{wang2024predictive}. \emph{Our interpretation:} given these
conventions and the named ``job CRD controller''~\cite{wang2024predictive}, they
are likely Kubernetes custom resources, as Palette's Feature and FeatureStore
are~\cite{uber2024palette}. The API is \emph{declarative}: users state the
desired result and controllers make reality match it~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{Offline data plane (L3a).} It ``does the heavy lifting on big data
processing'': features, training, evaluation and batch
inference~\cite{wang2024predictive}. Work runs as pipelines, DAGs of steps
executed on Spark or Ray~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{Online data plane (L3b).} It ``handles real-time model inference and
feature serving'' for Uber's other microservices~\cite{wang2024predictive}. The
Online Prediction Service (OPS) now uses Triton, and online features live in
Cassandra or Redis~\cite{wang2024predictive,uber2024palette}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Dependencies and Communication Between Layers}
\label{sec:layered-communication}

Dependencies point strictly \textbf{top-down}: upper layers command lower ones,
and lower layers never call upward. Information returns upward only as
\textbf{status} written back to control-plane resources (Kubernetes
convention~\cite{wang2024predictive}) or as \textbf{data} left in shared storage
(\Cref{fig:layered-communication}).

\begin{figure}[ht]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{memberD-fig5-2-communication}
  \caption[Dependencies and communication between the layers]{Dependencies and
    communication between the layers. Solid arrows are calls or commands;
    dashed arrows are status reports or data handed over through storage.}
  \label{fig:layered-communication}
\end{figure}

In \emph{our reconstruction} from the 2017 and 2024 posts, a request flows as
follows. An engineer submits a desired state (e.g.\ a Pipeline or Deployment)
from MA Studio or Canvas; controllers reconcile it, and job federation launches
Spark or Ray jobs on a suitable cluster~\cite{wang2024predictive}. Pipelines
write features to the offline store, and trained models are stored as new
versions in the model repository~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. Batch jobs load
features from HDFS into Cassandra, while streaming jobs aggregate Kafka events
into it~\cite{delbalso2017meet}. A controller then rolls the model out to OPS
with ``safe and incremental zonal rollout''~\cite{wang2024predictive}, and
product services call OPS over RPC~\cite{delbalso2017meet}.

Two observations follow (our reading of the sources). First, \textbf{the two data
planes never call each other}: they share data through storage and are
coordinated from above, so the online plane is independent of batch jobs.
Second, the control plane is \emph{closed}, since every change goes through its
declarative API, while the plug-and-play layer is partly \emph{open}: advanced
users can ``bring your own components''~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Other Architecture Styles Inside the Layers}
\label{sec:layered-other-styles}

Layering decides \emph{what may depend on what}; each layer then uses the style
that fits its job (\Cref{fig:layered-styles}).

\begin{figure}[ht]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{memberD-fig5-3-styles-in-layers}
  \caption[Other architecture styles placed in the layers]{Other architecture
    styles placed in the layers.}
  \label{fig:layered-styles}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Pipe-and-filter: offline data plane.} Pipelines are DAGs of
        steps, each consuming earlier outputs~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
  \item \textbf{Lambda: Palette, spanning both data planes} (\emph{our
        interpretation}). Batch and speed paths meet in a single serving
        store, Cassandra~\cite{delbalso2017meet}, matching Lambda's batch, speed
        and serving layers, although Uber never uses the term.
  \item \textbf{Event-driven reconciliation: control plane.} Its controllers
        react to resource changes, following the Kubernetes Operator
        pattern~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
  \item \textbf{Plugin (microkernel-like): plug-and-play layer.} Plug-and-play
        is one of Uber's design principles: stable entities hide
        interchangeable engines~\cite{wang2024predictive}.
\end{itemize}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Evaluation: How Well Does Layering Serve Michelangelo?}
\label{sec:layered-evaluation}

\paragraph{Benefit 1. Lower layers change without disturbing upper layers.}
Uber is migrating its clusters from Peloton/Mesos to Kubernetes and extending to
cloud GPUs; job federation hides cluster details for ``job
portability''~\cite{wang2024predictive}, so engineers keep submitting the same
pipelines while the infrastructure changes. This is the isolation the style
promises~\cite{richards2020}.

\paragraph{Benefit 2. Engines are swapped inside a layer.} Triton replaced Neuropod,
which is ``being deprecated'', in OPS, and Uber ``replaced Spark-based XGBoost and DL
trainers with Ray-based trainers \ldots{} for better scalability and
reliability''~\cite{wang2024predictive}. \emph{Our interpretation:} because teams
describe \emph{what} to train and deploy, not \emph{which engine} runs it, these
swaps stayed inside the lower layers. The same shared platform carried about 400
active projects and 5,000+ production models in 2024~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{Limitation 1. A fault in a shared lower layer can spread upward.} In
2021 a bad Palette metadata change, not caught because schema validation ran
only on the client, stopped online serving from loading metadata and broke major
Tier-1 use cases~\cite{uber2024palette}. Uber moved validation to the server and
added delta propagation, cutting end-to-end updates from ``over an hour'' to
about 15 minutes~\cite{uber2024palette}. \emph{Our interpretation:} a layer that
many others depend on needs stronger safeguards than any single caller.

\paragraph{Limitation 2. Extra hops cost latency} (\emph{our interpretation} of
Uber's data). Models that read features from Cassandra had a P95 target of under
10\,ms, against under 5\,ms for models that did not~\cite{delbalso2017meet}.

\paragraph{Limitation 3. Rigidity and cross-layer change.} Michelangelo 1.0's
config- and UI-driven path slowed iteration, which led Uber to add
PyML~\cite{delbalso2018scaling}, and the Spark-based feature DSL could not run on
GPUs~\cite{wang2024predictive}. Uber's answer was to open layers selectively
(Canvas, ``bring your own components'')~\cite{wang2024predictive}.

\paragraph{Overall assessment.} Layering isolates fast-changing infrastructure
and engines from hundreds of product teams, at the classic costs of fragile
shared layers, per-hop latency and rigidity. \emph{Our interpretation:} the move
from the loosely layered 1.0 to the explicit three-plane 2.0 suggests that a
large MLOps platform benefits from \emph{more} layering discipline over time,
not less.
